title: Weather & Climate Adventure: Processes
welcome_lead: Why does the BBC weather map have wiggly lines? Today we decode depressions, anticyclones and fronts.
meta_desc: GCSE Geography Weather processes — depressions, anticyclones, fronts, synoptic charts.
final_note: You can now interpret a synoptic chart and explain pressure systems.

concepts.def: Low pressure system — wet, windy, unsettled
High pressure system — calm, dry, clear skies
Warm air rises over cold air — steady rain
Cold air pushes under warm — heavy short rain
Line joining points of equal air pressure
Unit of air pressure — average sea level ~1013mb

walkthroughs.body_html:
Low pressure (depression): air rises, cools, condenses — cloud and rain. Common over the UK.

High pressure (anticyclone): air sinks, warms, dries — clear skies. Hot in summer, cold/frosty in winter.

A depression has two fronts:

Warm front (semicircles): warm air gently rises over cold — light, steady rain over hours.

Cold front (triangles): cold air aggressively undercuts warm — short, heavy thunderstorms.

Isobars are lines of equal pressure measured in millibars.

Closely packed isobars = strong winds. Widely spaced = calm. A central 'L' = depression; 'H' = anticyclone.
